solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: In Yorkshire town, large fruit's guarantee of freshness?

indicators.note: In places the next word's letter within the town just named, so it sits inside

parts.note: Selby is a market town in North Yorkshire
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
a date is a fruit; the 's is read as 'is', a link

explanation.surface: A query about whether a big fruit from a Yorkshire town comes with a promise that it is fresh.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'town' suggests a scene set in Yorkshire, but the town is wordplay; Selby is a market town in North Yorkshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: A sell-by date printed on food packaging tells shops the last day it may be sold, an assurance the item is fresh.

clue.text: Believer taking risks regularly in order to bring peace?

indicators.note: taking means the order to bring peace holds the next letters inside it

parts.note: 'sh!' is the command for quiet

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter of risks is taken

parts.note: the second and fourth letters of risks

explanation.surface: A believer who gambles in order to make peace, a paradox of a man of faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the even letters of risks, I and K, and 'taking' has SH (the order 'sh!') hold them.
explanation.definitionFit: A Sikh is a follower of Sikhism, a religious faith, so a believer by example.

clue.text: Volume of Poe's — maybe a line shows misprint

parts.note: Poe was American, and liter is the American spelling of the volume litre

explanation.surface: A volume of Poe's writing perhaps contains a printed line that betrays a typing slip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Volume' is not a book here but the measure: an American like Poe would write LITER, not litre. 'maybe' warns that this spelling is just one writer's.
explanation.definitionFit: Literal is a printers' term for a typographical error, a single wrong letter in the text.

clue.text: Repositioning hollow hidden log, lay back comfortably

indicators.note: Repositioning means the letters that follow are moved into a new order
hollow means the word is emptied, leaving only its outside letters

parts.note: first and last letters of hidden
taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone moves a hollow log that was hidden, then lies back at ease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hidden' looks like a hidden-word signal, but 'hollow' empties it to HN, which joins LOG, LAY and BACK to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom by a long chalk means by a wide margin, so winning comfortably or easily.

clue.text: Scorn drink after party

indicators.note: after means the drink comes behind the party in the answer

parts.note: a do is an informal word for a party
to down a drink is to swallow it

explanation.surface: Someone sneers at the idea of having a drink once the party is over.
explanation.definitionFit: To do someone down is to belittle or disparage them, treating them with contempt.

clue.text: Chap runs, first to board public transport

indicators.note: to board means to get on, so the letters go inside the vehicle

parts.note: a tram is a form of public transport
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
1st, written as IST with the figure read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A man dashes to be the first passenger to get on a tram or bus.
explanation.walkthrough: First is written 1ST, and the 1 is read as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Tristram is a man's given name, as in the knight of Arthurian legend, so an example of a fellow.

clue.text: Composer's "very loud" alternative?

parts.note: or introduces an alternative
ff, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: A musician's piece is offered as a loud alternative to something quieter.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is read as 'is'. Carl Orff wrote Carmina Burana, a famously loud piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Carl Orff was a German musician who wrote Carmina Burana, so an example of a composer.

clue.text: Pole with fiddle meeting old composer

parts.note: a rod is a pole
to rig is to fiddle or fix dishonestly

explanation.surface: A Polish violinist meets an elderly musician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' and 'fiddle' suggest a Polish violinist; they are a rod and a rig.
explanation.definitionFit: Joaquín Rodrigo was the Spanish musician who wrote the Concierto de Aranjuez, so an example of a composer.

clue.text: What'll silence buzzer going off initially when tyre's flat

indicators.note: going off means the letters explode into a new order
initially means only the first letter of the word is used

parts.note: first letter of when
taken as written, letters TYRES
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something that stops a buzzer going off, at the moment a tyre goes flat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'buzzer' suggests an alarm, and 'going off' fits that picture, but it is the anagram signal; the buzzer is a fly.
explanation.definitionFit: A flyswatter is a flat paddle for killing insects, and a dead fly stops its buzzing.

clue.text: Christopher to give up ringing his first relatives

parts.note: Kit is a short form of the name Christopher

indicators.note: ringing means surrounding, so the letter sits inside the phrase

parts.note: to hand in is to give up or surrender
his refers back to Christopher, whose first letter is K

explanation.surface: A man named Christopher is told to stop phoning his family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ringing' looks like phoning; it means encircling. 'his first' is the first letter of Christopher, K.
explanation.definitionFit: Kith and kin is an idiom for friends and family together, everyone one is connected to.

clue.text: Tight component in maladjusted gyroscope

indicators.note: component in says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A tight part inside a badly adjusted gyroscope.
explanation.definitionFit: Tight and edgy both describe being tense and nervous, so they are synonyms in that sense.

clue.text: Get behind trees overlooking motorway briefly and peer, mostly unseen

indicators.note: overlooking means in this down clue the trees sit above the next letters

parts.note: to back something is to get behind it, support it
woods are groups of trees
M is the abbreviation for motorway, as in the M1

indicators.note: briefly means the word is cut short, losing its last letter

explanation.surface: Instructions to hide in trees above a motorway and peer out unseen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peer' looks like a verb, to look; it is a noun, a lord. A backwoodsman is a hereditary peer who rarely attends the House of Lords, Britain's upper chamber.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage a backwoodsman is a member of the House of Lords who seldom turns up to sit there.

clue.text: Film of aviator, one whom we sent flying

indicators.note: sent flying means the letters are scattered and land in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A film about a pilot, someone we launched into the air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flying' suits the aviator picture, but 'sent flying' is the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A Room with a View is the 1985 Merchant Ivory movie made from E. M. Forster's novel.

clue.text: Assume nothing about a Lord Fauntleroy?

indicators.note: about means going round, so the first two pieces surround the rest

parts.note: to don is to put on or assume
a duck is a score of nothing in cricket

explanation.surface: Don't assume anything about a Lord Fauntleroy, the boy hero of the old novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lord Fauntleroy' points to the Victorian children's book Little Lord Fauntleroy, but only Fauntleroy is the definition: it is the cartoon duck's middle name. A duck is a zero score in cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: The Disney cartoon character Donald Duck's middle name is Fauntleroy, a piece of trivia.

clue.text: Favour one make

definitions.meaning: first meaning: do someone a favour

explanation.walkthrough: 'one make' reads like a car model; the clue splits into two senses of the same verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both doing a kindness for someone and compelling them by duty or law.

clue.text: Raise profit as symbol of oppression

parts.note: to jack up is to raise, as with a car on a jack
boot is an old word for profit or advantage, as in 'to boot'

explanation.surface: Raising profits is seen as the mark of a tyrannical regime.
explanation.walkthrough: Boot meaning profit survives in the phrase 'to boot', meaning in addition.
explanation.definitionFit: The jackboot, a tall military boot worn by Nazi troops, stands for authoritarian rule.

clue.text: Good uniform one found tossed in vermin-infested tip

indicators.note: tossed in means thrown into the next word, so the letters go inside

parts.note: ratty can mean overrun with rats
U is uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A good uniform is found thrown away in a rubbish tip crawling with rats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tip' looks like a rubbish dump, completing the scene, but it is the definition: a gratuity.
explanation.definitionFit: A gratuity is money given to a waiter or helper for service, the same as a tip.

clue.text: Not slow as Liberal Left to put in a sympathetic word

indicators.note: to put in means the two letters are placed inside the words that follow

parts.note: 'there, there' is said in sympathy

explanation.surface: Not a slow party: the Liberals left a kind word in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'there, there' is a comforting phrase, so THERE is a sympathetic word; L and L go inside A THERE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone all there is mentally alert and sharp, the opposite of dim-witted.

clue.text: Drop holiday travel

parts.note: leave is time off work, a holiday
to go is to travel

explanation.surface: Holiday travel falls off.
explanation.definitionFit: Leave go is an informal way of saying let go, to release something gripped.

clue.text: Sailor's secure? He might get the sack

parts.note: PO, Petty Officer, is a naval rank, plus the S of the possessive
to tie is to secure

explanation.surface: A sailor asks whether his job is safe, given he might be fired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get the sack' means be fired, but here it is literal: a postie is the British informal word for a postman, who carries a mail sack.
explanation.definitionFit: A postie, British slang for a mail carrier, is given a bag of letters to deliver.

clue.text: Couple beginning to talk without notes

indicators.note: beginning to means only the opening letter of the word is taken

parts.note: first letter of talk
w/o is a written abbreviation for without
so and me are notes of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A pair starts to talk without any notes in front of them.
explanation.walkthrough: SO and ME are two notes of the tonic sol-fa (do, re, me, fa, so).
explanation.definitionFit: A twosome is a pair of people together, the same as a couple.

clue.text: I'm cool? The opposite, if not PC!

indicators.note: if not says the answer minus these letters gives the other part, so they belong inside it

parts.note: the opposite of cool is heat
taken as written, the abbreviation for politically correct

explanation.surface: Someone claims to be cool, while being anything but, unless politically incorrect.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue works backwards: without the letters PC the answer would be the opposite of cool, so those letters belong inside that opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: A hepcat is a dated slang term for a hip, stylish jazz fan, someone who would say they are cool.

clue.text: Number dash to secure E European espionage facility

indicators.note: to secure means to hold, so the first word keeps the next inside it

parts.note: number read as more numb, i.e. deader
a Lett is a Latvian, from Eastern Europe
a dash of liquid is a drop

explanation.surface: A digit and a dash secure a phone number for an Eastern European spy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' is not a figure but numb-er, more numb, so DEADER.
explanation.definitionFit: A dead-letter drop is a hiding place where spies leave messages to be collected without meeting.

clue.text: At college, a small tree

parts.note: to be up is to be in residence at university

explanation.surface: On a university campus there is a little tree.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage you go up to university, and are up while there.
explanation.definitionFit: The upas is a poisonous tree of Java, an example of a tree.

clue.text: They're strung up and kept, equally securely, at the front

indicators.note: at the front means the leading letter of each word is taken

parts.note: first letter of up
first letter of kept
first letter of equally
first letter of securely

explanation.surface: Things are hung up and stored evenly and safely at the front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strung up' suggests hanging; 'strung' alone is the definition, and UP starts the word picks.
explanation.definitionFit: Ukes, short for ukuleles, are small guitars fitted with strings.

clue.text: Fool's new pay cut works both ways

indicators.note: cut means the word is shortened, losing its last letter

parts.note: income is pay
OP, opus, means works; written backwards then forwards gives PO then OP

explanation.surface: An idiot's fresh pay cut goes both ways.
explanation.walkthrough: OP is short for opus, a musical work; read both ways it gives PO then OP.
explanation.definitionFit: A nincompoop is a silly or foolish person, the same as an idiot.

clue.text: Aloud, runs down old preacher

indicators.note: Aloud means the answer is spoken, so it only sounds like the phrase

parts.note: to knock is to run down or criticise, so knocks

explanation.surface: Someone speaks out against an elderly clergyman.
explanation.definitionFit: John Knox was the sixteenth-century Scottish reformer who led the Presbyterian church, a famous minister.

clue.text: Witnesses what's written beneath title of saintly Swede's book?

parts.note: under a book's title comes 'by' and the author's name
ST is the abbreviation for saint
the Swede who wrote the book is given a common Swedish first name, Anders

explanation.surface: Witnesses to whatever is printed under the title of a holy Swede's work.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the fanciful picture: a book by a Swedish saint would print 'by St Anders' under its title.
explanation.definitionFit: Bystanders are people who happen to see an event, the same as onlookers.
